en: To regard with disgust and hatred
hook: AB-HOR: so HORrible that you back AWAY from it.
story: Abhor. Walking home from class, Nadia saw three boys throwing stones at a thin, limping stray dog. Something inside her snapped. She marched over, scolded them so fiercely that they ran, then carried the trembling dog to an animal shelter two kilometres away. Nadia abhors cruelty to animals. To abhor is to hate something deeply, with disgust. It is stronger than dislike. Think: something so horrible that you pull back from it.

gre.s: Although the novelist claimed to ____ violence, critics noted that her books dwell on it in loving, almost gleeful detail.
gre.clue: dwell on it in loving, almost gleeful detail

en: Noisy, energetic, and cheerful; rowdy
hook: BOISTEROUS: BOYS-terous, a room full of loud, playful boys.
story: Boisterous. On Eid morning, Grandma's house fills with twenty cousins. They race up and down the stairs, shout across rooms, wrestle on the sofa, and play cricket in the hallway with a rolled-up newspaper. A vase wobbles; an uncle shouts; everyone laughs louder. Nobody can hear the TV. The cousins are boisterous: noisy, energetic, and cheerful, a little rowdy. Boisterous crowds celebrate loudly. Picture a room full of boys being boys.

gre.s: The usually ____ classroom fell completely silent when the principal walked in unannounced.
gre.clue: fell completely silent

en: Courteous, gallant, and honorable, especially toward women
hook: CHIVALROUS: like a medieval knight's CHIVALRY.
story: Chivalrous. The bus from Mirpur was packed. An elderly woman climbed on with heavy bags and nowhere to sit. A young man in a university T-shirt immediately stood up, offered her his seat, held her bags, and later helped her step down at her stop. Passengers smiled at each other. His behaviour was chivalrous: courteous, gallant, and honourable, especially toward women. The word comes from chivalry, the code of medieval knights.

gre.s: In an age of cynicism, the soldier's ____ treatment of his captured enemies, whom he fed and sheltered, astonished his comrades.
gre.clue: whom he fed and sheltered

en: Rude and bad-tempered in a mean-spirited way
hook: CHURLISH: a grumpy CHURL who growls at everyone.
story: Churlish. Tanvir's friends secretly planned a birthday party for him: balloons, cake, and a slideshow of embarrassing photos. When he walked in and everyone shouted "Surprise!", he frowned. "I hate surprises." He ate one slice of cake, thanked nobody, and left after ten minutes. His friends were stunned. His behaviour was churlish: rude, bad-tempered, and ungracious. It would be churlish to refuse a sincere gift. A churl was once a rude peasant.

gre.s: It would be ____ to criticize the volunteers' modest fundraiser, given how generously they had donated their own time.
gre.clue: given how generously they had donated their own time

en: Kept secret or done secretively, especially because it is illicit
hook: CLANDESTINE: a secret CLAN meeting in the DESTINY hour of midnight.
story: Clandestine. During the 1971 war, freedom fighters met in village huts at midnight, whispering plans by the light of a single candle. Messages were hidden in rice sacks and passed by children who looked like they were playing. If discovered, everyone would be arrested or worse. Their meetings were clandestine: secret, hidden, usually because they are forbidden. A clandestine operation, a clandestine affair. Think of a secret clan meeting under the stars.

gre.s: The two rival companies held ____ talks for months, keeping the negotiations hidden even from their own boards of directors.
gre.clue: keeping the negotiations hidden even from their own boards

en: Self-satisfied and unaware of possible dangers or shortcomings
hook: COMPLACENT: so COMfortable in their PLACE that they stop trying.
story: Complacent. After scoring 318 on his first practice test, Arif felt brilliant. He stopped reviewing vocabulary. He played video games every evening. "I've got this," he told everyone. On the real test, he scored 301. Overconfidence had made him careless. He had become complacent: smugly self-satisfied, unaware of dangers and weaknesses. Complacency is the enemy of success. Think: so comfortable in your place that you stop trying.

gre.s: Having won the championship three years in a row, the team grew ____, skipping practices and underestimating opponents they once feared.
gre.clue: skipping practices and underestimating opponents

en: Large, heavy, and difficult to carry or use; slow and complicated
hook: CUMBERSOME: it ENCUMBERS you.
story: Cumbersome. Moving the old wooden almirah down four floors of a narrow staircase in Old Dhaka took six men, three hours, two broken railings, and one sprained ankle. It was enormous, heavy, and impossible to turn around corners. Later, Lamia tried to renew her trade license: twenty forms, five offices, and three stamps. That process was cumbersome too. Cumbersome means awkward and hard to handle because of size, weight, or complexity. Think: it encumbers you.

gre.s: Engineers replaced the ____ old filing system, which required three separate forms for every request, with a simple online portal.
gre.clue: which required three separate forms for every request

en: Causing serious weakness or incapacity
hook: DE-BILITATE: removes your ABILITY.
story: Debilitating. When Mitu caught dengue, the fever lasted a week. The weakness lasted a month. She could not climb the stairs to her flat without stopping twice. She could not hold a book for more than ten minutes. Even her favourite food tasted like cardboard. The illness was debilitating: causing serious weakness and making normal life impossible. Debilitating migraines, debilitating anxiety, debilitating injuries. Think: it removes your ability.

gre.s: For years she suffered from ____ migraines, which sometimes confined her to a dark room for days at a time.
gre.clue: confined her to a dark room for days at a time

en: Done consciously and intentionally (adj.); to think carefully before deciding (verb)
hook: DELIBERATE: done with LIBERTY of choice, on purpose.
story: Deliberate. With five minutes left and his team winning by one goal, the defender grabbed the opposing striker's shirt and pulled him to the ground. It was no accident. It was a deliberate foul to stop a certain goal. The referees then deliberated for ten minutes before showing a red card. As an adjective, deliberate means intentional, or slow and careful. As a verb, to deliberate means to think carefully before deciding.

gre.s: Investigators concluded that the fire was not an accident but a ____ act, pointing to traces of fuel poured near every exit.
gre.clue: pointing to traces of fuel poured near every exit

en: Amusing in a dry, odd, or whimsical way
hook: DROLL: a DOLL that makes funny, dry jokes.
story: Droll. At his ninetieth birthday party, a young relative asked Grandfather how it felt to be so old. He thought about it seriously. "Like an old car," he said, with a perfectly straight face. "Everything still works. Except the engine. And the wheels. And the brakes." The room exploded with laughter, but he did not even smile. His humour was droll: amusing in a dry, quiet, slightly odd way. Droll comedians never laugh at their own jokes.

gre.s: The memoir's ____ observations, delivered with a perfectly straight face, had readers laughing at the most mundane details of office life.
gre.clue: had readers laughing

en: Unconventional and slightly strange
hook: EC-CENTRIC: off-center, not in the middle like everyone else.
story: Eccentric. Professor Haque wears mismatched shoes on purpose, brings a pet parrot to his physics lectures, eats his lunch standing on a chair, and writes equations on his kitchen walls. He once gave a lecture entirely in rhyme. His students adore him. He is eccentric: unconventional and slightly strange. Ec means out, centric means centre: literally off-centre, not in the middle like everyone else. Many geniuses have been famous eccentrics.

gre.s: The billionaire was known for his ____ habits, such as wearing a raincoat indoors and dining only on food that was blue.
gre.clue: wearing a raincoat indoors and dining only on food that was blue

en: Irritable and quarrelsome; hard to control
hook: FRACTIOUS: always creating FRACTURES in the group.
story: Fractious. The apartment building's committee met every month to decide simple things: the guard's salary, the lift repairs, the Eid decorations. Every meeting became a battle. Members interrupted each other, formed rival groups, stormed out, and refused to agree on anything. A one-hour meeting took four. The committee was fractious: irritable, quarrelsome, and hard to control. A fractious toddler throws tantrums when tired. Think: it keeps creating fractures in the group.

gre.s: The coalition was notoriously ____, its members squabbling so constantly that it rarely managed to pass any legislation at all.
gre.clue: its members squabbling so constantly

en: Completely clear and transparent; easy to understand
hook: LIMPID: clear as a LIMPID pool where you can see the bottom.
story: Limpid. At Bichanakandi, a stream flows down from the hills of Meghalaya so clear that Sara could see every pebble on its bed, every tiny fish darting between the stones, even a ring someone had dropped long ago. Later, her guide explained the region's history in a few simple, beautiful sentences that anyone could follow. Both the water and his words were limpid: completely clear and transparent. Synonyms: lucid, pellucid.

gre.s: Unlike his convoluted early essays, the philosopher's later works are written in ____ prose that even beginners can follow.
gre.clue: that even beginners can follow

en: Sentimental in an exaggerated or false way
hook: MAWKISH: makes you want to say 'mock-ish', sickly sweet.
story: Mawkish. The TV drama's final episode lasted three hours. Every scene had slow-motion tears, violins swelling dramatically, characters declaring their feelings in long speeches, and a puppy appearing at sad moments. Viewers who began crying soon began rolling their eyes instead. It was mawkish: sentimental in an exaggerated, false, sickly way. A mawkish greeting card is so sugary it makes you wince. It tries too hard to make you feel.

gre.s: The critic praised the film for treating its tragic subject with restraint, avoiding the ____ excesses of earlier versions that had wallowed in tearful melodrama.
gre.clue: wallowed in tearful melodrama

en: Deep respect or a gesture expressing it, such as a bow
hook: OBEISANCE: OBEY + bow down.
story: Obeisance. When the old music master entered the room, his students rose, bowed their heads, and touched his feet, the traditional gesture of respect for a guru. He placed a hand on each head in blessing. Later, a visiting foreigner asked what the gesture meant. A student explained: obeisance. Obeisance means deep respect, or a gesture expressing it, such as a bow. Courtiers paid obeisance to the king. Think: obey and bow down.

gre.s: Courtiers were expected to perform elaborate ____ before the emperor, bowing until their foreheads touched the floor.
gre.clue: bowing until their foreheads touched the floor

en: Showy and designed to impress or attract attention
hook: OSTENTATIOUS: 'OSTEN-TATIOUS', 'Look at me, look at my stuff!'
story: Ostentatious. The businessman arrived at the village fair in a gold Lamborghini, wearing three gold chains, a diamond watch, and sunglasses, though it was evening. He handed out thousand-taka notes and made sure the cameras filmed every one. The villagers stared at the car stuck in the muddy road. His display was ostentatious: showy and designed to impress or attract attention. Ostentation is flashy display. The opposite is understated.

gre.s: Though enormously wealthy, the philanthropist lived without ____ display, driving an old car and living in a modest house.
gre.clue: driving an old car and living in a modest house

en: A solution or remedy for all problems
hook: PAN-ACEA: PAN = all. A cure for ALL.
story: Panacea. Before the election, the candidate promised a single giant bridge would solve everything: traffic jams, unemployment, poverty, floods, and even corruption. Economists laughed. A bridge is a bridge; it cannot fix a whole economy. He was selling a panacea: a supposed remedy for all problems. Pan means all, as in pandemic. On the GRE, authors often warn that no single policy is a panacea for complex problems.

gre.s: Although technology can help, experts caution that it is no ____ for the deep social problems that affect the nation's schools.
gre.clue: the deep social problems

en: Done with minimal effort, routinely and without real interest
hook: PERFUNCTORY: done just to PERFORM the FUNCTION, nothing more.
story: Perfunctory. Imran's grandmother waited three hours to see the doctor. He glanced at her for one minute, asked two questions without looking up, scribbled a prescription, and called the next patient. He never read her test results. The checkup was perfunctory: done with minimal effort, routinely, without real interest. Think: done only to perform a function, nothing more. A perfunctory smile, a perfunctory apology, a perfunctory inspection.

gre.s: The manager gave the report only a ____ glance before signing it, a carelessness that allowed several glaring errors to slip through.
gre.clue: allowed several glaring errors to slip through

en: Full of danger or risk
hook: PERILOUS: full of PERIL.
story: Perilous. Every monsoon, the children of a char village on the Brahmaputra cross a fast-flowing channel to reach their school. They squeeze into a small, overloaded wooden boat, the water inches below its edge, with no life jackets. One wrong wave could capsize it. Their parents pray each morning. The journey is perilous: full of danger or risk. Peril means serious danger. A perilous situation could turn deadly at any moment.

gre.s: Despite warnings that the mountain pass was ____ in winter, the travelers set out without guides and were soon trapped by an avalanche.
gre.clue: were soon trapped by an avalanche

en: Spreading widely throughout an area or group
hook: PERVASIVE: PERVADES everything, like a smell filling a house.
story: Pervasive. Farhan's mother fried onions for the evening's biryani. Within minutes, the smell had spread into every room, every curtain, every pillow, even the clothes in his cupboard. Two days later, his shirts still smelled of onions. The smell was pervasive: spreading widely throughout an area. Corruption can be pervasive too, seeping through every level of an organisation. Pervasive is close to ubiquitous. Think: it pervades everything.

gre.s: Researchers found the influence of social media so ____ that it shaped nearly every aspect of teenagers' daily lives.
gre.clue: shaped nearly every aspect of teenagers' daily lives

en: To prevent from happening; to make impossible
bn: আগেই রোধ করা; অসম্ভব করে তোলা
hook: PRE-CLUDE: CLOSE the door BEFORE it can happen.
story: Preclude. Zayan dreamed of joining the army since he was six. At eighteen, he passed every written exam with top marks. Then the medical test found an old knee injury from a cricket match. The rules were clear: the injury precluded him from serving. To preclude is to prevent something in advance, making it impossible. Pre means before, clude means close: closing the door before you can walk through. His busy schedule precluded any holiday.

gre.s: The patient's weak heart may ____ surgery, forcing doctors to consider gentler forms of treatment.
gre.clue: forcing doctors to consider gentler forms of treatment

en: A special liking or preference for something
hook: PRE-DILECTION: PRE-selected as your DELIGHT.
story: Predilection. Mitu puts green chili on everything: in her eggs, in her noodles, on her mango slices, even, once, on ice cream. Her friends cry when they share her food. She just smiles and adds more. She has a predilection for spicy food: a strong preference or liking. Predilection usually describes a taste or fondness, while proclivity often suggests a bad tendency. Think: pre-selected as your delight.

gre.s: The collector's ____ for small Dutch landscapes was well known, and dealers saved such paintings especially for him.
gre.clue: dealers saved such paintings especially for him

en: Aggressively greedy; grasping
hook: RAPACIOUS: like a RAPTOR, a bird of prey grabbing everything.
story: Rapacious. Over twenty years, a powerful landlord in one district grabbed land from poor farmers: forged documents, bribed officials, and sent thugs to threaten anyone who resisted. Field by field, he took nearly the whole village. Whatever he owned, he wanted more. He was rapacious: aggressively, ruthlessly greedy, seizing whatever he could. Picture a raptor, a bird of prey, swooping down and grabbing everything below. Rapacious companies exploit nature without limit.

gre.s: The ____ developers bulldozed protected wetlands to build luxury resorts, ignoring both the law and the protests of local residents.
gre.clue: bulldozed protected wetlands

en: To enjoy greatly; great enjoyment
bn: উপভোগ করা; তৃপ্তি সহকারে গ্রহণ করা
hook: RELISH: like a delicious RELISH sauce you savor.
story: Relish. After a year studying in Germany eating bread and pasta, Rafi came home to Dhaka. His mother placed a plate of shorshe ilish, hilsa fish in mustard sauce, in front of him. He ate slowly, closing his eyes with every bite, savouring every flavour. He relished it: enjoyed it greatly. You can also relish a challenge, relish a victory, or relish the chance to prove someone wrong. Think of a delicious relish sauce.

gre.s: Far from dreading the debate, the candidate seemed to ____ the chance to confront her opponent in front of a national audience.
gre.clue: Far from dreading the debate

en: Using humor, irony, or exaggeration to criticize people's foolishness
hook: SATIRICAL: SATIRE makes fun of the powerful.
story: Satirical. Every Friday night, a comedy show on TV portrays the country's politicians as cartoon characters fighting over a giant cake. One minister falls into the icing; another steals the cherry. The audience laughs. The politicians grumble. But behind the jokes is a serious point about greed. The show is satirical: using humour, irony, and exaggeration to criticize people's foolishness or vice. Satire has a serious message hidden behind the laughter.

gre.s: The magazine's ____ cartoons, which exaggerated the president's vanity to absurd lengths, made him a laughingstock across the country.
gre.clue: exaggerated the president's vanity to absurd lengths

en: Something that is not what it pretends to be; fake
hook: SHAM: a SHAMe, a fake.
story: Sham. A new charity appeared after the floods, collecting money in every market and on every social media page. Donations poured in. Months later, journalists discovered that not a single taka had reached flood victims. It had all paid for the founders' cars and flats. The charity was a sham: something that is not what it pretends to be, a fraud. The trial that followed was also a sham; the verdict had been decided in advance.

gre.s: Critics dismissed the election as a ____, noting that opposition candidates had been banned and the results announced before the polls closed.
gre.clue: the results announced before the polls closed

en: To go around the edge of; to avoid dealing with an issue
hook: GRE trick: to SKIRT means to go around the edge, like a skirt's hem.
story: Skirt. The highway into town was flooded, so the bus skirted the town centre, taking the outer road around its edge. That evening, a journalist asked the mayor about the flooded roads. The mayor talked about new parks, cricket results, and tourism, but never once about the flooding. He skirted the question. To skirt is to go around the edge of something, or to avoid dealing with a difficult topic. Picture walking along the hem of a skirt.

gre.s: Rather than addressing the scandal directly, the spokesperson tried to ____ the issue by talking at length about the company's charitable work.
gre.clue: Rather than addressing the scandal directly

en: Slow-moving, inactive, or lacking energy
hook: SLUGGISH: as slow as a SLUG.
story: Sluggish. After a heavy lunch of rice, dal, and beef curry, Tanvir felt sluggish all afternoon: heavy body, slow thoughts, every email taking twice as long. The country's economy that year was sluggish too, with businesses barely growing and few new jobs. Sluggish means slow-moving, inactive, or lacking energy. A sluggish computer takes forever to open a file. Picture a slug crawling slowly across a garden path.

gre.s: Despite heavy government spending, the economy remained ____, growing at barely one percent for the third straight year.
gre.clue: growing at barely one percent for the third straight year

en: Showing simplicity and a lack of luxury; austere
hook: SPARTAN: like the warriors of SPARTA, tough and simple.
story: Spartan. The national cricket team's training camp in the hills was famously spartan: thin mattresses on concrete floors, cold showers at five in the morning, plain rice and lentils for every meal, and absolutely no phones. Some young players almost quit in the first week. By the end, they were tough, focused, and fitter than ever. Spartan means simple, plain, and lacking comfort. The ancient Spartans were famous for their harsh, disciplined lifestyle. Synonym: austere.

gre.s: The monks' ____ quarters contained nothing but a narrow cot, a wooden stool, and a single candle.
gre.clue: contained nothing but a narrow cot, a wooden stool, and a single candle

en: Eager to argue or fight; aggressively defiant
hook: TRUCULENT: like a TRUCK driver ready to fight anyone in traffic.
story: Truculent. A bus driver scraped a car in Farmgate traffic. Instead of apologizing, he jumped out, shouting and waving his fists, ready to fight anyone who came near. The car's owner backed away. Passengers sighed; this happened every week with him. He was truculent: eager to argue or fight, aggressively defiant. Truculent is a close synonym of belligerent and pugnacious. Picture a truck driver ready to fight everyone on the road.

gre.s: The ____ witness refused to answer even routine questions, glaring at the prosecutor and threatening to walk out of the courtroom.
gre.clue: glaring at the prosecutor and threatening to walk out
